title: Hunger and thirst ask for a place (1.2)
hook: once the gods have moved in, two more voices speak up: hunger and thirst want a home too
tomorrow: the self enters through the crown of the head

segments.voice: Yesterday: the person, the house the gods called well made, with fire in the mouth and the moon in the heart. Your line was the gods within.

Everyone's moved in. Fire has the mouth, the sun has the eyes, the moon has the heart. The house is full and humming. Then there's a knock. Two figures stand outside, and they were there before the gods arrived. In fact, they're why the gods went house-hunting at all. Their names are hunger and thirst, ashanaya and pipasa, and they say to the self: what about us? Find us a place too. You know these two: mid-afternoon, midnight at the fridge, long meetings. The Aitareya gives them a whole verse.
screen: `THE HOUSE IS FULL.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `HUNGER AND THIRST: WHAT ABOUT US?`

segments.voice: Here's the order in the story. When the gods first fell into the great ocean, the self touched that whole creation with hunger and thirst. That's why the gods asked for a home: they wanted a place to eat. So hunger and thirst are older than the house. They didn't break in. They were part of the plan. Now, with the gods settled, the two ask: find a place for us. The self doesn't banish them, or scold them as enemies of the spirit. It says, more or less: I'll give you a share among these gods. You'll be partners with them. That's why, the text explains, whenever an offering is made to any god, hunger and thirst share in it. An ordinary arrangement, and a generous one. One way to hear it: when your eyes see, they get hungry for more seeing. When your ears hear a song, they want the next one. When the mind, the moon in the heart, settles on an idea, it gets thirsty for another. On this reading, every power comes with an appetite. Some later teachers read the passage as a sober account of the human condition: wanting runs through every sense. But the story itself is calm about it. Nobody is shamed for being hungry. The self knows who lives in the house, and gives each one its share.
screen: `HUNGER AND THIRST WERE THERE FIRST.` · `THEY ASK: FIND US A PLACE.` · `A SHARE IN EVERY GOD'S OFFERING.` · `EVERY POWER COMES WITH AN APPETITE.` · then, large: `THEY TOO NEED A HOME.`

segments.voice: Check gently for hunger, thirst, or some other wanting: for your phone, for news, for this to be over. Don't obey it and don't fight it; just find where it lives in the body, the stomach, the throat, the hands. Let it sit there, known and given room, without running the house.
Appetite, the hunger and thirst that ask the self for a place. In the Aitareya, they're given no room of their own, but a share in whatever is offered to every god.
Your line: they too need a home. In this story, even wanting gets a seat. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Teachers of the Aitareya read this passage when explaining why appetite goes with every sense, and in Vedic ritual each offering is made to a particular deity, the share the passage says hunger and thirst join.
